1.pericope_label: Hear ye now what the Lord saith; Arise, contend thou before the mountains, and let the hills hear thy voice. Hear ye, O mountains, the Lord’s controversy, and ye strong foundations of the earth: for the Lord hath a controversy with his people, and he will plead with Israel.

schools.summary: Ellicott calls the opening a solemn appeal to nature to hear the Lord pleading with his people, and points to the older song that opens by giving ear to heaven and earth. Keil and Delitzsch describe the chapter as a judicial contest between the Lord and his people: their ingratitude for great blessings held up, then the demand of righteousness and love and a humble walk in place of outward sacrifice, and last the punishment their violence and lying make necessary.

Gill reports the figurative reading without dismissing it, that the chief men of the land may be meant, who stood as pillars to uphold the common people. Calvin refuses that reading, holding that those who find judges figuratively pointed out here may be easily refuted; his account is that the prophet had spent much labour on the people and derived no fruit, so he is at length bidden to call the mountains to bear their testimony, the reproach being that the elements, destitute of reason as they are, had more understanding than these men. He adds a point of manner distinguishing this prophet from two others who did the same: they addressed the heavens and the earth abruptly, whereas this one prefaces his discourse by saying the summons was specially committed to him.

Clarke sets the chapter out as a dialogue with the parts assigned: God speaks the first five verses, the people deprecate his judgments in the sixth and seventh, in the eighth God prescribes the way they are to be saved, and from the ninth to the end the prophet remonstrates. He calls the manner of raising attention awakening and sublime, and explains why it was necessary, God having spoken to priests, princes and people and done everything needful to make them wise and happy, and been uniformly disobeyed. Wesley says the mountains are the mountains properly so called, and that the sin was so notorious that the whole creation might be summoned as a witness.

Henry offers a third possibility for the mountains and declines it: the address may be to the inhabitants of those hills, and some think the hills on which they worshipped idols are intended, but he judges it better taken generally. He finds two purposes in the command: to excite the earnestness of the prophet, who must speak as vehemently as if he designed to make the hills hear him; and to expose the people's stupidity, since the rocks that have no ears must hear where Israel, which has ears, will not. He adds that what the prophet speaks he speaks in God's name, so they are bound to hear it not as the word of a dying man but of the living God.

debates.question: Are the mountains literal or figurative?

positions.position: Literal: the mountains properly so called, summoned as witnesses.
Possibly the chief men of the land, who stood as pillars to the people.
Not the judges figuratively: those who find them here may be easily refuted.
Possibly the inhabitants of the hills, or the hills of idol-worship, but better taken generally.

debates.question: Why are the elements summoned at all?

positions.position: Because the prophet's labour on the people had borne no fruit, so the elements must testify and shame them by having more understanding.
To excite the prophet's earnestness and to expose the people's stupidity at once.
Because their ingratitude was enough to make the mountains hear and tremble and give judgment.

outliers.claim: Distinguishes this prophet's manner from that of two others who summoned the heavens and the earth abruptly, since this one first prefaces his discourse by saying the summons was specially committed to him, so that his hearers might know something altogether unusual was coming.

themes: Hear ye now what the Lord saith; Arise, contend thou before the mountains, and let the hills hear thy voice.
Hear ye, O mountains, the Lord’s controversy, and ye strong foundations of the earth: for the Lord hath a controversy with his people, and he will plead with Israel.

3.pericope_label: O my people, what have I done unto thee? and wherein have I wearied thee? testify against me. For I brought thee up out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed thee out of the house of servants; and I sent before thee Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. O my people, remember now what Balak king of Moab consulted, and what Balaam the son of Beor answered him from Shittim unto Gilgal; that ye may know the righteousness of the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott is interested in the pause rather than the persons: Israel, abashed, makes no answer, so the Lord continues to plead, the naming of the family to whom the decree was committed being his reply. On the hired diviner he makes it the strongest instance available, there being no more conclusive case extant of a man's will controlled to do the exact opposite of what he intended; he would put a full stop after the diviner's answer and make what follows an independent instance; and he holds the last word means liberality or beneficence rather than righteousness. Keil and Delitzsch put it plainly, that Israel cannot deny these gracious acts, and the memory of them recalls the ingratitude that repaid them.

Gill turns the address into the aggravation, that they were a people chosen above all others, redeemed from bondage and loaded with benefits, and sinned against him nonetheless. Calvin says it seems unbecoming that God should stand ready like a guilty man to clear himself, and explains it as a concession, a personification ascribing to God a character not his own; the address doubles their wickedness, since God descends from his own elevation and takes the opposite side as though the question were to be discussed between friends. On the diviner he explains why that one story is singled out, the stream of mercy having seemed stopped when a prophet came forth armed as with celestial weapons against them.

Clarke calls the condescension astonishing and puts it as a plea in court: they are called to show why sentence should not be pronounced, and if their answer is reasonable they shall be heard first; they are silent, and God states what he has done for them. He assigns each of the three names an office, leader and lawgiver, priest, and prophetess to direct the women, supported from the Chaldee; and on the two places he takes the phrase of the interval in which the different answers were given. Wesley asks what injustice has been done and what burdensome impositions laid on them, reads the two places of the length of the king's border along which the debauching continued, and makes the last word mercy, justice and veracity together.

debates.question: What does the phrase naming two places refer to?

positions.position: The interval in which the diviner gave his different answers, the camp advancing towards the river.
An independent instance: put a full stop after the diviner's answer, and what follows recalls the spies and the passage of the river.
Neither: the first place is where the women of Midian were used to debauch Israel, and the phrase marks the length of the king's border along which it continued.

debates.question: What does the closing word mean?

positions.position: Liberality or beneficence rather than righteousness.
Mercy, justice and veracity together.

outliers.claim: Explains that God's offer to answer a charge is a concession and a personification, a character not his own being ascribed to him, since the prophet could not otherwise express that nothing blameable could be found in him.

themes: O my people, what have I done unto thee? and wherein have I wearied thee? testify against me.
For I brought thee up out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed thee out of the house of servants; and I sent before thee Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.
O my people, remember now what Balak king of Moab consulted, and what Balaam the son of Beor answered him from Shittim unto Gilgal; that ye may know the righteousness of the Lord.

6.pericope_label: Wherewith shall I come before the Lord, and bow myself before the high God? shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves of a year old? Will the Lord be pleased with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of rivers of oil? shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?

schools.summary: Ellicott reports the view that these are a Moabite king's questions, quoting a modern dean on a short dialogue preserved not by the historian of the law but by this prophet, and then sets it aside as less in harmony with the context than the conscience-stricken reply of the people impersonated in some earnest speaker; on the last offer he allows an allusion to real human sacrifices. Keil and Delitzsch state the function of the passage rather than its detail: the outward means of reconciliation are set up so that the next verse may overthrow them and recall the people to the moral demands of the law.

Gill denies outright that these are the words of the people God had a controversy with, since what is proposed suits no such character even if the speakers were hypocrites, and makes them the Moabite king's questions to the diviner; he keeps the rams within the same reading, as what that king had himself offered. Calvin takes two things as granted, that the people are without excuse and that God had contended with them only to restore them, since had the purpose been merely to condemn there would have been no need of such questions; whenever God chides his people he opens to them the door of hope, provided those who have sinned repent.

Clarke has the people appear as defendants and plead guilty at once, and he grades the offers as they rise: the burnt offerings are reasonable and according to the law but insufficient, the thousands of rams might be procured though with difficulty, the rivers of oil are absurd and impossible, and the last offer is not merely useless but sinful, though such sacrifices were made by two neighbouring peoples and copied by the corrupt among Israel. Wesley reaches the same conclusion in a line, that a man whose heart was touched by the foregoing expostulation may be supposed to make the enquiry.

Henry dwells on the enquirers. Judgment having been given against them and their guilt being too plain to deny and too great to excuse, they desire peace on any terms, and apply to the right person, the prophet by whose ministry they had been convinced; for who is fitter to show them the way than the man who made them sensible of having missed it. He notices that each speaks for himself, asking not what this man shall do but what he himself shall do, since every one knows the plague of his own heart.

positions.position: Not the people at all but the Moabite king, putting questions to the diviner.
The people, appearing as defendants and pleading guilty at once.
The people, impersonated in some earnest speaker; the Moabite reading is reported and set aside.
A man whose heart was touched by the foregoing expostulation.

debates.question: What are the escalating offers for?

positions.position: They rise from the lawful to the impossible to the sinful, and conscience refuses each in turn.
They are the disguise of men who will not come directly to God, the way having been easily knowable.
They are set up so that the next verse may overthrow them.

outliers.claim: Quotes a modern dean who writes of a short dialogue preserved not by the historian of the law but by this prophet, exhibiting the agony of the king and the lofty conceptions of the seer, and then sets that whole reading aside as less in harmony with the context.

themes: Wherewith shall I come before the Lord, and bow myself before the high God? shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves of a year old?
Will the Lord be pleased with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of rivers of oil? shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?

8.pericope_label: He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the Lord require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?

schools.summary: Ellicott is the briefest of the four and answers by two parallels: the principle that God sets more by mercy than by sacrifice, and the close of another book, where the conclusion of the whole matter is to fear God and keep his commandments, since this is the whole of man. He treats the three requirements as the sum of what is asked rather than a reduction of it.

Gill, having made the two preceding verses a Moabite king's questions, makes this the diviner's answer to him, a single man who had consulted him; and though a king, he was no more than a man, and that duty the Lord had shown him by the light of nature, which is the work of the law written in the heart. Calvin comes at the evasion from the other end: hypocrites inquire how God is to be pacified as though very solicitous, and the whole enquiry is a disguise, since by circuitous windings they turn aside and never wish to come directly to God, being wilfully blind at midday and smothering the light of the law that should have directed their steps.

Clarke takes the address as universal and divides the three requirements, subdividing the first into three creditors: God, who is owed heart, body, soul and spirit in the love that takes the whole strength; the neighbour, owed what one would wish done to oneself; and the man himself, whose body must be kept in temperance. To love mercy goes beyond justice into kindness and charity, and the third clause tells how the other two are done, the Hebrew implying that one humbles oneself in order to walk, since without that humiliation there never was and never can be any walking with God.

positions.position: A single man, the Moabite king, who is reminded that though a king he is no more than a man.
Everyone: it is the answer to the failed offers, since no mode of expiation can purify from guilt.

debates.question: Does the verse reduce religion to three moral duties?

positions.position: No: many parry every exhortation with this very text, and the question is whether they are willing to stand or fall by it.
No: the enquiry it answers was itself a hypocrite's disguise, the law having already shown enough and more than enough.
The three are the sum of what is asked, as elsewhere fearing God and keeping his commandments is the whole of man.

outliers.claim: Turns on the readers who use this verse against the doctrine of sin and atonement, shutting their eyes to both and parrying every exhortation with it on the ground that God requires nothing but to do justly, love mercy and walk humbly; his answer is to ask any such man whether he is willing to stand or fall by it.

themes: He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the Lord require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?

9.pericope_label: The Lord’s voice crieth unto the city, and the man of wisdom shall see thy name: hear ye the rod, and who hath appointed it. Are there yet the treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked, and the scant measure that is abominable? Shall I count them pure with the wicked balances, and with the bag of deceitful weights? For the rich men thereof are full of violence, and the inhabitants thereof have spoken lies, and their tongue is deceitful in their mouth.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the city for the metropolis of the wealth and sinfulness of Judah, reads seeing the name as regarding it and suggests the sentence may be parenthetical, renders the measure as the hateful ephah of leanness, would read the balances clause as asking whether God himself can be innocent with such scales, and says the fraud was practised by men who had not even the pitiable excuse of poverty. Keil and Delitzsch keep the city and identify it with the capital, refusing to take the opening words as a separate exclamation, and put the emphasis on the little word yet, which stands before the interrogative particle for that reason.

Gill reports the rendering to awaken alongside the city, takes the treasures for wealth collected unlawfully and kept instead of restored to those defrauded, reports two further renderings of the opening words, and notes of the rich men that they had enough of the world and no temptation to do an ill thing for money. Calvin sets out the grammar for the second rendering, that the word may be derived from another root and read as a verb meaning to arouse, and prefers it, since the people were torpid and as it were overpowered with sleep; he uses the verse to complain that he and the other teachers did little, though God designed his voice to be heard from the least to the greatest, and the song was sung to the deaf.

Clarke alone maps the sins that follow onto the three requirements: the treasures of wickedness and the false balances show that they were not doing justly, the violence of the rich men that they did not love mercy, and the lies of the inhabitants that they had not humbled themselves to walk with God. Wesley extends the address to every city while making the capitals principal, and gives the little word yet its force, that this continued after so many laws and examples of punishment.

Henry makes the clause about wisdom a definition: when the voice of God cries to us we may by it see his name, and it is a point of true wisdom to discover the name of God in his voice and learn what he is from what he says, though many are not aware of it because they do not regard it. He adds why the crying comes first: God warns before he wounds, being unwilling that any should perish.

debates.question: Does the voice cry to the city or cry to awaken?

positions.position: To awaken: the word may come from another root, and the people were torpid and overpowered with sleep.
To the city, the capital, with the opening words joined to what follows.
To every city, with the two capitals principal.

debates.question: What is the force of the clause about the balances?

positions.position: That God will not count such men pure or reckon them just.
Rather, can God himself be innocent with deceitful balances, the law having stringently required just weights.

outliers.claim: Maps the three sins condemned in these verses onto the three requirements of the preceding verse, so that the false balances answer to doing justly, the violence of the rich to loving mercy, and the lies of the inhabitants to walking humbly with God.

themes: The Lord’s voice crieth unto the city, and the man of wisdom shall see thy name: hear ye the rod, and who hath appointed it.
Are there yet the treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked, and the scant measure that is abominable?
Shall I count them pure with the wicked balances, and with the bag of deceitful weights?
For the rich men thereof are full of violence, and the inhabitants thereof have spoken lies, and their tongue is deceitful in their mouth.

13.pericope_label: Therefore also will I make thee sick in smiting thee, in making thee desolate because of thy sins. Thou shalt eat, but not be satisfied; and thy casting down shall be in the midst of thee; and thou shalt take hold, but shalt not deliver; and that which thou deliverest will I give up to the sword. Thou shalt sow, but thou shalt not reap; thou shalt tread the olives, but thou shalt not anoint thee with oil; and sweet wine, but shalt not drink wine. For the statutes of Omri are kept, and all the works of the house of Ahab, and ye walk in their counsels; that I should make thee a desolation, and the inhabitants thereof an hissing: therefore ye shall bear the reproach of my people.

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that the word rendered thy casting down occurs nowhere else, derives it from an unused root meaning to be void, and offers hunger as a translation; he has them collecting their property for flight and failing; and he turns aside at the olives to explain that oil was indispensable for personal comfort, supporting its standing from the old parable of the trees taking counsel about a king, in which the olive was reckoned first, before even the vine and the fig. Keil and Delitzsch render it that God has smitten them with an incurable sickness.

Gill takes the judgments of famine, pestilence and war to waste the state as a diseased body, and traces the first of the two kings named at the close from captain of the army to the throne, having him build the capital and set up an idolatrous worship established by laws and edicts; the aggravation lies in the distance of time, those statutes being still kept many years after, and royal authority is no excuse against the command of God. Calvin alone explains where the threatened losses come from, the prophet having taken his words from the lawgiver, since the prophets, when they wished greater authority, quoted the curses of the law literally.

Clarke proposes that the opening clause is perhaps better read as God himself being weary with smiting, having corrected them to no purpose; he reports a bishop's emendation transposing two letters to read that it shall be dark, which he thinks probably the true reading; he calls the first king one of the worst they ever had and the son's wife a woman without fellow on earth; and he closes with a judgment on the chapter, that few in the prophets or anywhere are superior to it for genuine worth. Wesley says the strokes will reach the heart until Israel is heartsick of its wounds, keeps the received text at the disputed word and turns it inward, and notes that the reproach is the one named in the law for a people who forsake God.

debates.question: Who is made sick by the smiting?

positions.position: The people, wasted by famine, pestilence and war as a diseased body wastes.
The people, but struck to the heart until they are heartsick of their wounds.
Perhaps God himself, weary with smiting to no purpose.
The people, smitten with an incurable sickness.

debates.question: What does the rare word in the fourteenth verse mean?

positions.position: It occurs nowhere else and comes from an unused root meaning to be void, so it may be rendered hunger.
The text should be emended by transposing two letters to read that it shall be dark, which the Arabic and Greek appear to support.
The received text stands: they shall be cast down at home and by their own hands.

outliers.claim: Closes the chapter with a literary judgment, that few chapters in the prophets or in the whole Bible are superior to this for genuine worth and importance, its structure being as elegant as it is impressive.

themes: Therefore also will I make thee sick in smiting thee, in making thee desolate because of thy sins.
Thou shalt eat, but not be satisfied; and thy casting down shall be in the midst of thee; and thou shalt take hold, but shalt not deliver; and that which thou deliverest will I give up to the sword.
Thou shalt sow, but thou shalt not reap; thou shalt tread the olives, but thou shalt not anoint thee with oil; and sweet wine, but shalt not drink wine.

For the statutes of Omri are kept, and all the works of the house of Ahab, and ye walk in their counsels; that I should make thee a desolation, and the inhabitants thereof an hissing: therefore ye shall bear the reproach of my people.
